slides.text: Operators combine values into new ones. Here you do arithmetic, update a variable in place, compare values, join conditions with logic, work on bits and join strings. The snippet is a map of the operators, not Go.
slides.code:
arithmetic  + - * / %
compare     == != < <= > >=
logic       && || !
update      += -= *= /= ++ --
bits        & | ^ &^ << >>
text        +

exercises.title: Arithmetic
exercises.guide: Combine two whole numbers with the five arithmetic operators.

chunks.guide: Two whole numbers to work with.
`+`, `-` and `*` work as in maths. `a` and `b` themselves do not change.
`/` on two whole numbers gives a whole number: the decimals are cut off. `%` gives the remainder of the division.

notes.text: What is left over after dividing.
Whole-number division: decimals are cut off.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: Two ints divide into an int, cut toward zero: 3 and -3. Converting `a` to `float64` first makes the division exact: 3.5.

exercises.title: Update a variable
exercises.guide: Change a variable with shorthand operators and print the result.

chunks.guide: A number to update.
`+=` adds to the variable itself, and `*=` multiplies it. `count += 5` means `count = count + 5`.

notes.text: Adds to the variable in place.
Multiplies the variable in place.

chunks.guide: `++` adds 1. In Go it is a statement on its own line.

notes.text: Adds one to the variable.

chunks.guide: Print the final value.

exercises.title: Increase by one
exercises.guide: Add one to `count` with Go's increment operator.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    count := 1
    count___
    fmt.Println(count)
}

exercises.title: Compare and combine
exercises.guide: Compare a number, then join the results with logic.

chunks.guide: A number to compare.
A comparison gives a `bool`: `>=` is true when the left side is bigger or equal.

notes.text: True when the left side is at least the right.

chunks.guide: `||` is true when either side is true.

notes.text: True when either side is true.

chunks.guide: `&&` needs both sides true, and `!` flips a bool.

notes.text: True when free is false.
True only when both sides are true.

chunks.guide: Print the three bools.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    open := true
    broken := false
    ready := false
    fmt.Println(open || broken && ready)
    fmt.Println((open || broken) && ready)
}
exercises.explanation: `&&` binds tighter than `||`, so the first line is `open || (broken && ready)`: true. The parentheses in the second change the grouping: `true && false` is false.

slides.text: A number is stored as bits. Bitwise operators work on each bit of two numbers at once. The snippet is pseudo code, with 12 and 10 written in bits.
Shifts slide all the bits. `<<` moves them left, which doubles the number for each place. `>>` moves them right, which halves it and drops the rest.
Two more things to know: `%` keeps the sign of its **left** side, and `&&` and `||` stop early. When the left side already decides the answer, the right side never runs. Last, `+` also joins strings.

exercises.title: Bitwise operators
exercises.guide: Combine the bits of two numbers.

chunks.guide: In bits, 12 is `1100` and 10 is `1010`.
`&` keeps the bits that are 1 in both: `1000`. `|` keeps the bits that are 1 in either: `1110`. `^` keeps the bits that are 1 in only one: `0110`.

notes.text: Xor: a bit that differs between the two.
And: the bits set in both numbers.
Or: the bits set in either number.

chunks.guide: `&^` clears from `a` every bit that is 1 in `b`: `1100` becomes `0100`.

notes.text: And not: a single operator in Go.

exercises.title: Shift the bits
exercises.guide: Move the bits of a number left and right.

chunks.guide: Two numbers to shift.
`n << 1` moves the bits one place left, so the number doubles. `n << 3` doubles it three times.

notes.text: Moves the bits left: doubles the number.

chunks.guide: `>>` moves the bits right. Each place halves the number, and the bits that fall off are lost.

notes.text: Moves the bits right: halves the number.

exercises.title: Shift left
exercises.guide: Shift `n` left by two bits, so the program prints 12.

exercises.title: Remainder of a negative
exercises.guide: See which sign `%` gives when a number is negative.

chunks.guide: A negative number and a positive one.
`/` cuts toward zero, so `-7 / 3` is -2. The remainder is what is left: -1.
The sign of `%` follows the **left** side. A positive left side gives a positive result, and the right side's sign does not matter.

notes.text: Left is negative, so the result is too.

exercises.title: Stop early
exercises.guide: Guard a division so it never runs when `b` is zero.

chunks.guide: `b` is zero, so `a / b` would crash the program.
`&&` is false as soon as its left side is false, so the right side is never evaluated. There is no division, and no crash.

notes.text: The guard: it goes on the left.
True when the two sides differ.

chunks.guide: `||` does the same when its left side is true: the right side is skipped.

notes.text: True when the two sides are equal.

exercises.title: Why this order?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick what `b != 0 &&` is for.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    a := 10
    b := 0
    ok := b != 0 && a/b > 1
    fmt.Println(ok)
}
options: Checks that b is a valid number before it is used
Makes both comparisons run, so each one is checked
Skips a/b when b is zero, so it cannot crash
Turns the result of a/b into a bool
exercises.explanation: When `b != 0` is false, `&&` already knows the result and never evaluates `a/b`. Swap the sides and the division runs first.

exercises.title: Join strings
exercises.guide: Build a sentence by joining strings with `+`.

chunks.guide: Two strings to join.
On strings, `+` joins them into a new string. Spaces and punctuation are strings too.

notes.text: On text, + joins the pieces into one string.

chunks.guide: `+=` works on strings as well: it adds to the end.

notes.text: Adds the text to the end of the variable.

chunks.guide: Print the result.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `+` on two strings joins them: "55". On two numbers it adds: 10.
